turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. How have you been getting on?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah sure I'm grand. Well, I'm not grand, the breathing's been desperate. I was supposed to be at the match, the Dubs, and I couldn't get up the hill to the stop without hanging onto the wall.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): That sounds rotten. Tell me in your own words what's been going on with the chest.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, it started as a cold, the usual dose, sneezing and a scratchy throat, and then the wheeze came in behind it. I'd say it's been two weeks... no, it was the Tuesday before last, so more like ten days.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Ten days sounds right. I'm his carer, I stay in the house Monday to Friday. The cold has been easing, but the wheeze got worse as it eased, if that makes sense.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): It does. When the wheeze is on you, what else do you notice?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The chest goes tight, like someone parked a bag of coal on it, worse at night. I'm coughing as well, a dry cough, keeps me awake. I was up at three watching videos of dogs, which is mad, I know.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever in this, or are you bringing up phlegm that's green or yellow?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. And nothing's coming up, it's a dry cough. My mam has a whole theory about green phlegm but I haven't got that.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He hasn't been hot. I put a hand on him a few evenings and he was grand.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been using for the asthma? The inhalers, walk me through them.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I've a blue one and a brown one and I mix them up, to be honest with you. I thought the brown one was for when you're gasping, so I've been reaching for that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You've it backwards, love. The blue is the reliever, the salbutamol. The brown is the preventer you're meant to take every day, even on the good days.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that right? God, my head's melted. So the blue one, I've been on that maybe five, six times a day, two puffs each go. The brown one's been sat on the windowsill doing nothing.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. Blue salbutamol, two puffs, maybe five or six times a day. And the brown one, do you know the name on the box?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Clenil, I think. It says two hundred... no, I looked this morning, the box says one hundred micrograms. Two puffs morning and night, when I remember. Which I haven't, since the cold.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was taking it before all this. Since the cold he's basically stopped the brown one. I leave it by the toothbrush and it doesn't move.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets, or anything from the chemist?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol now and again, for the head. That's the lot. Oh, the bus was a disaster today, we were stood in the rain twenty minutes, I was going to complain but sure who would I even ring.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): The rain won't have helped the chest, right enough. Any allergies to medicines, that you know of?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. I had penicillin years ago for a throat and I was grand with it.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There's nothing written up on the sheet at the house either.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the asthma itself, how long have you had it? Has it ever put you in hospital?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was a small lad, primary school. Usually not a bother if I take the brown one. I had a bad spell two winters ago and they gave me the steroid tablets. Never in hospital with it, though.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or is there smoke in the house?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. I tried one cigarette at a wedding and I coughed for a week, never again. My cousin smokes but he doesn't live with us. He's a character, he'd talk the hind leg off a donkey.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The house is smoke-free. He usually walks the dog most days, a collie, but he's been skipping that since the chest got bad.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Bran, yeah. Mad as a brush. I was supposed to book his booster at the vet and I forgot, that's been on my mind more than the inhalers, which says it all.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave Bran to the vet. Let me have a listen, if you sit forward a bit.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's a wheeze through both lungs, no crackles, and you're talking away in full sentences, which is a good sign. The nurse read your peak flow outside, she called three hundred and ten... no, I'm looking at the chart, it's three hundred and forty litres a minute. Your best on the card is five hundred and twenty.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Three forty? That's brutal. I can usually get past five hundred when I'm well. Is that why the hill nearly killed me?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's well down on your best, yes. I think this is the asthma flaring up after the cold, not a chest infection. The dry cough and no fever fit with that.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So no antibiotic? My uncle gets one every time he coughs and he's evangelical about it in the family chat. I nearly texted him a photo of the waiting room.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't give you an antibiotic for this. What I do want is a short course of steroid tablets. Prednisolone, thirty milligrams... no, we'll make it forty milligrams by mouth once a day for five days, with your breakfast.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Forty, once a day, five days. I'll see that he takes them. Will they leave him wired? He's college work piled up.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): They can make you a bit hungry or restless. Five days is usually grand. And I want you back on the brown inhaler properly, two puffs morning and night, and the blue one only when you're actually tight, not on a schedule.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): If I'm needing the blue one all day, like I have been, that's too much, is it?

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is, yeah. If you're still needing it more often than every four hours once the tablets are in, ring us or get seen. And use a spacer if you've one. It gets more of the puff into the lungs.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): There's a spacer under the bed with the odd socks. I'll fish it out. I keep saying I'll tidy that room.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. And the serious bit, so you have it: if you can't finish a sentence, or the blue inhaler isn't touching the wheeze, or anyone notices a blue tinge at the lips, that's A&E, don't sit on it.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. I don't feel that bad. I walked in, apart from the hill and the rain and the bus, which is a saga.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sitting here you're not in trouble. I don't need a chest x-ray today. We might do one if this hasn't settled, but not now.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And do we come back, or only ring if he dips?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks, and we'll check the peak flow again. If you're worse before that, don't wait for the appointment.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, grand. Are the steroid ones the little white tablets? I had some before that were pink, or white, I genuinely can't remember.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): They'll be five milligram tablets, so eight of them each morning makes the forty. The chemist will label the box. Don't go by the colour.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight tablets. Right. Sorry for the rambling, the inhalers do my head in.
[SEG0048] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll write it on the fridge. Blue when you're tight, brown morning and night, tablets five mornings.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perfect. Are you tighter now than when you walked in, or much the same?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Much the same. Bit wheezy, not gasping. The night cough is the annoying part.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Prop yourself up a bit at night, it can ease that cough. I'm not adding any other medicine today. I can do a short note for college if you missed anything.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I missed a lab yesterday, yeah, a note would be class. Thanks.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll leave it with reception on your way out. Mind yourself, and don't let Bran drag you up that hill till the chest has settled.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Caregiver does not state college attendance; patient mentions college work and missed a lab.
Sneezing and scratchy throat after Tuesday before last are stated, but not clearly current now.

The cold symptoms were easing while the wheeze was worsening as the cold improved.
Dry cough was severe enough to keep him awake at night; he was up at 3 a.m. because of it.
No medication allergy history included that he had taken penicillin previously without any reaction.
History of previous asthma exacerbation treated with steroid tablets two winters ago.
House is smoke-free / no smoke exposure in the home.
Peak flow of 340 L/min was well down from personal best of 520 L/min on his card.
Doctor advised no antibiotic for this episode.
Prednisolone to be taken with breakfast.
Doctor specified prednisolone would be 5 mg tablets, taking 8 tablets each morning to make 40 mg.
Doctor said no chest x-ray is needed today.
At reassessment, symptoms were 'much the same', bit wheezy but not gasping; night cough remained the main troublesome symptom.
Doctor stated he was not adding any other medicine today.
Follow-up plan included checking peak flow again at the two-week review.
